title: Contract for SR&ED - Canadian R&D Tax Credit Glossary
description: Read our Canadian glossary to learn what constitutes a valid Contract for SR&ED and who retains the right to claim R&D tax credits.
summary: A contract for SR&ED is an agreement under which a contractor performs SR&ED work in Canada on a claimant's behalf. Under the Income Tax Act, arm's-length contract payments enter the Section 37 pool in full but earn investment tax credits on only 80%, while non-arm's-length contract payments earn no payer credit unless Form T1146 transfers qualified expenditures.

body.text: A contract for SR&ED is an agreement under which a contractor performs SR&ED work in Canada on a claimant's behalf. Under the Income Tax Act, arm's-length contract payments enter the Section 37 pool in full but earn investment tax credits on only 80%, while non-arm's-length contract payments earn no payer credit unless Form T1146 transfers qualified expenditures.

This report delivers a comprehensive technical audit and reference guide to Canada's federal, provincial, and territorial research and development (R&D) tax incentive framework, written in Canadian English and grounded in primary Canadian statutes, Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) policies, Department of Finance budgetary papers, and Tax Court of Canada / Federal Court of Appeal jurisprudence as of November 2026.

Canada's primary fiscal mechanism for supporting industrial innovation is the federal Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Program, administered by the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) alongside tax policy oversight from the Department of Finance Canada. Governed by subsection 248(1), Section 37, and Sections 127 and 127.1 of the federal Income Tax Act (R.S.C., 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.)) and Part XXIX of the Income Tax Regulations (C.R.C., c. 945, Sections 2900–2903), the program provides two complementary incentives: first, an immediate 100% income tax deduction (or indefinite carryforward) for allowable current and capital SR&ED expenditures pooled under subsection 37(1); and second, a volume-based Investment Tax Credit (ITC) under Sections 127 and 127.1 ranging from a 15% basic rate to an enhanced 35% refundable rate on qualified SR&ED expenditures. When stacked with provincial and territorial R&D tax incentives—including Québec's unified 20% to 30% Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC), British Columbia's permanent 10% SR&ED tax credit, Ontario's 8% Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC) and 3.5% Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC), Alberta's 8% to 20% Innovation Employment Grant (IEG), Saskatchewan's 10% R&D tax credit, and the 15% to 20% refundable credits across Manitoba, Atlantic Canada, and the Yukon—qualifying Canadian claimants can recover a substantial share of eligible R&D costs in combined federal and provincial assistance.

Between December 2024 and 2026, Canada enacted the most significant legislative expansion of the SR&ED program in more than a decade. Initially proposed in the 2024 Fall Economic Statement, expanded in the November 4, 2025 federal budget (Budget 2025), and enacted into law via Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1), which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026, these reforms apply retroactively to taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024. Specifically, Bill C-15 doubled the annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% refundable ITC from $3 million to $6 million (increasing the maximum annual refundable federal credit from $1.05 million to $2.1 million), widened the prior-year taxable capital phase-out range for Canadian-controlled private corporations (CCPCs) from $10 million–$50 million to $15 million–$75 million, extended access to the 35% enhanced refundable ITC to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) using a three-year average consolidated gross revenue phase-out ($15 million to $75 million, which CCPCs may also elect to use), and restored the eligibility of capital expenditures and equipment lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024. Additionally, on April 1, 2026, the CRA launched an optional Pre-Claim Approval Process (using Form T1322), offering upfront technical eligibility determinations within eight weeks and cutting expenditure review processing times in half from 180 days to 90 days. Most recently, Budget 2026 proposed further expansions to bring regulatory certification testing and intellectual property (IP) registration and maintenance expenses within the scope of eligible SR&ED claims for taxation years beginning on or after Budget Day.
1. Legislative Architecture and Dual-Incentive Mechanics
1.1 Primary Statutory Authorities under the Income Tax Act and Regulations

The statutory architecture of the federal SR&ED program rests on four interconnected segments of the federal Income Tax Act and the Income Tax Regulations. First, subsection 248(1) (Definitions) establishes the substantive legal definition of "scientific research and experimental development"—which was moved from subsection 2900(1) of the Income Tax Regulations into subsection 248(1) of the Act in 1996, with Regulation 2900(1) formally repealed by SOR/2000-296, s. 1—alongside essential definitions for "salary or wages" and "specified employee".

Second, Section 37 (Scientific Research and Experimental Development Deduction Pool) governs the calculation and pooling of allowable current and capital SR&ED expenditures carried on in Canada under subsection 37(1) and outside Canada under subsection 37(2). Within Section 37, subsection 37(1.2) sets out the available-for-use requirement for capital property; subsection 37(1.3) extends domestic treatment to SR&ED performed in the exclusive economic zone of Canada (within the meaning of the Oceans Act) or the airspace, seabed, or subsoil above or below that zone; and subsections 37(1.4) and 37(1.5) establish the 10% limit on permissible salaries and wages for SR&ED performed outside Canada. Furthermore, subsection 37(4) prohibits any deduction for expenditures made to acquire rights in, or arising out of, SR&ED; subsection 37(6.1) restricts the deduction of pre-acquisition pool balances following a loss restriction event; subsection 37(8) interprets eligible current, capital, and lease expenditures and governs the annual election between the Traditional and Proxy overhead methods; subsections 37(9) to 37(9.4) prohibit bonuses or profit-based remuneration for specified employees and cap their claimable SR&ED salary at five times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) across associated corporations; subsections 37(11) and 37(12) enforce the mandatory 18-month reporting deadline for prescribed forms; and subsection 37(13) governs non-arm's-length SR&ED contracts.

Third, Sections 127 and 127.1 (Investment Tax Credit and Refundable Investment Tax Credit) govern the calculation, application, carryover, recapture, and cash refundability of the SR&ED ITC. Specifically, subsection 127(5) permits the deduction of non-refundable ITCs from Part I federal tax payable and governs the 3-year carryback and 20-year carryforward mechanics; subsection 127(8) governs the allocation of partnership ITCs to members; and subsection 127(9) codifies the statutory definitions of "investment tax credit", "qualified expenditure", and "government assistance". Subsections 127(10.1) to 127(10.6) establish the enhanced 35% ITC rate, the expenditure limit formula, and the associated-corporation allocation rules; subsections 127(11.1) to 127(11.8) and 127(18) to 127(20) mandate reductions to qualified expenditures for government assistance, non-government assistance, and contract payments; subsections 127(13) to 127(16) regulate non-arm's-length qualified expenditure transfers and cost caps; subsections 127(27) to 127(36) impose ITC recapture upon the sale or commercial conversion of SR&ED property; and Section 127.1 authorizes the cash refund of earned ITCs to eligible claimants.

Fourth, Part XXIX of the Income Tax Regulations (Sections 2900 to 2903) provides the regulatory mechanics for cost attribution and proxy overhead. Subsection 2900(2) defines current expenditures "directly attributable" to the prosecution of SR&ED (materials consumed or transformed, salaries and wages of employees directly undertaking, supervising, or supporting SR&ED, and other expenditures directly related and incremental to the prosecution); subsection 2900(3) defines expenditures directly attributable to the provision of premises, facilities, or equipment; subsection 2900(4) sets the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) at 55% of the eligible salary base; subsection 2900(5) establishes the "all or substantially all" (90% or more) rule for employee salaries; subsection 2900(6) caps the PPA at overall net business deductions; subsections 2900(7) to 2900(9) establish the specified employee proxy salary base limits (75% of total salary and 2.5× YMPE) and exclude bonuses, profit-based remuneration, and taxable benefits; Section 2901 addresses prescribed expenditures; and Section 2903 defines special-purpose buildings.
1.2 The Two-Stage Computational Structure: Section 37 Pool vs. Section 127 Qualified Expenditures

A core tenet of Canadian R&D tax compliance is that "allowable SR&ED expenditures" added to the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool and "qualified SR&ED expenditures" eligible to earn an ITC under Section 127 are calculated independently in Part 3 and Part 4 of Form T661. As tax practitioners emphasize, an expenditure can be deductible in the Section 37 pool without generating an ITC in the same amount, meaning audit working papers must never treat "SR&ED expenditure" and "qualified expenditure" as interchangeable terms.

Under subsection 37(1) and the CRA's Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures Policy (updated March 30, 2022), a taxpayer carrying on business in Canada aggregates allowable current and post-December 15, 2024 capital SR&ED expenditures into a cumulative deduction pool. Deductions from the Section 37 pool are optional: a claimant may deduct any amount up to the available pool balance (Form T661 Line 455) in the current taxation year (Line 460) to reduce net income for tax purposes, or carry forward any undeducted balance (Line 470) indefinitely to offset taxable income in future taxation years. However, two statutory restrictions constrain the Section 37 pool carryforward. First, because a partnership is not a separate taxpayer and computes its net income at the partnership level under subsection 96(1), a partnership cannot carry forward a Section 37 pool balance to a subsequent fiscal period; the entire pool balance at year-end must be deducted in full in computing the partnership's net income for the year. Second, if a corporation or trust undergoes a loss restriction event (such as an acquisition of control), subsection 37(6.1) restricts the deduction of pre-acquisition pool balances so that they may only be deducted in subsequent years against income from the business in which the SR&ED was carried on or a similar business. Furthermore, under subsection 37(4), no deduction is allowed for any expenditure made to acquire rights in, or arising out of, SR&ED—regardless of whether the performer previously claimed SR&ED or was a non-resident—because only the actual performer of the R&D in Canada is entitled to the tax incentive.

By contrast, Section 127 computes the Investment Tax Credit based on "qualified expenditures" defined in subsection 127(9) and totalled on Line 570 in Part 4 of Form T661. Five major structural adjustments distinguish the Section 127 qualified expenditure base from the Section 37 deductible pool:

items: Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA): When a claimant elects the Proxy Method under clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B), the notional overhead amount (55% of the eligible salary base under Regulation 2900(4)) is added to qualified expenditures on Line 502 of Form T661 to earn an ITC, but is never added to the Section 37 deduction pool because actual overhead expenses are deducted as ordinary business expenses.

Arm's-Length Subcontracts and Third-Party Payments: While 100% of an eligible arm's-length SR&ED contract expenditure (Line 340) or third-party payment (Line 370) enters the Section 37 pool, subparagraph (a)(ii) of "qualified expenditure" in subsection 127(9) restricts the ITC base to 80% of those expenditures, requiring a 20% reduction on Line 529 of Form T661.

Non-Arm's-Length (NAL) Subcontracts: Payments under an SR&ED contract to a non-arm's-length performer enter the payer's Section 37 pool on Line 345, but are excluded from the payer's qualified expenditures on Line 541 under paragraph (f) of "qualified expenditure" in subsection 127(9), unless the performer and payer jointly file Form T1146 to transfer the performer's qualified expenditures to the payer (reported on Line 508).

Used Capital Equipment: Under the restored capital expenditure rules effective after December 15, 2024, acquiring used (second-hand) depreciable property intended for 90% or more SR&ED use in Canada qualifies for the Section 37 deduction pool, but is a prescribed expenditure disallowed from earning an ITC and must be deducted on Line 530 of Form T661.

Shared-Use Equipment (SUE): Depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024 that is used primarily (more than 50% but less than 90% of its operating time) for SR&ED in Canada cannot be claimed in the Section 37 deduction pool, but 25% of its capital cost qualifies for the SR&ED ITC in the first period (first-term SUE) and 25% in the second period (second-term SUE) under subparagraph (a)(iii) of "qualified expenditure" in subsection 127(9).

body.text: 1.3 Summary of 2024–2026 Federal Legislative Reforms (Bill C-15, Bill C-69, and Budget 2026)

Tax auditors reviewing Canadian SR&ED claims across 2024, 2025, and 2026 must account for the chronological sequence of recent federal legislative enactments. Initially, the 2024 Fall Economic Statement and the Department of Finance's August 15, 2025 legislative proposals proposed increasing the enhanced 35% ITC expenditure limit from $3 million to $4.5 million, widening the CCPC taxable capital phase-out to $15 million–$75 million, extending the 35% refundable credit to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs), and restoring capital expenditure and lease cost eligibility after December 15, 2024. Subsequently, the federal budget tabled on November 4, 2025 (Budget 2025) further increased the annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% ITC from the proposed $4.5 million to $6 million, effective retroactively for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024. All of these measures were enacted into law via Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1), which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026. Additionally, Bill C-69 (reflected in CRA policy updates on January 28, 2025) amended the definition of "government assistance" in subsection 127(9) so that bona fide loans from public authorities in Canada with reasonable repayment terms made after December 31, 2019 are generally no longer treated as government assistance that grinds the SR&ED pool.

Most recently, Budget 2026 proposed two major commercialization and intellectual property expansions applicable to taxation years beginning on or after Budget Day, carrying an estimated federal fiscal cost of $930 million over five fiscal years ($25 million in 2026–2027, $200 million in 2027–2028, $245 million in 2028–2029, $225 million in 2029–2030, and $235 million in 2030–2031). First, under the Regulatory and Certification Requirements measure, eligible SR&ED activities will expand to include tests, technological validations, and studies conducted to meet regulatory requirements needed to obtain initial approval or certification necessary for commercializing a product or process, provided those activities relate directly to an eligible SR&ED project (with wages, materials, contracts, overhead, and machinery/equipment claimable under existing rules). Second, under the Intellectual Property (IP) Protection measure, eligible expenditures will expand to cover costs reasonably incurred to prepare, file, obtain, and periodically maintain protection for eligible IP—specifically patents, certificates of supplementary protection, plant breeders' rights, and copyrighted software under Canadian or equivalent foreign legislation—developed during an eligible SR&ED project. While administrative fees payable to foreign IP offices are eligible, supporting preparation activities qualify only if conducted in Canada, litigation or IP enforcement expenses are excluded, and recapture rules will apply to both the SR&ED deduction and ITC if the taxpayer subsequently disposes of the IP.

body.text: 2. Substantive Definition of SR&ED and Technical Eligibility Criteria
2.1 Statutory Text and Structure of Subsection 248(1)

Eligibility for both the Section 37 deduction and the Section 127 ITC is governed by the statutory definition of "scientific research and experimental development" in subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act, which generally aligns with the OECD Frascati Manual while restricting eligible domains to the natural sciences and engineering. Under subsection 248(1), SR&ED is defined as a "systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis" that falls into one of three core research categories (paragraphs (a), (b), or (c)), includes eight specific types of commensurate support work (paragraph (d)), and excludes seven enumerated commercial or non-scientific activities (paragraphs (e) to (k)).

Among the three core categories, paragraph 248(1)(a) (Basic Research) covers work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view, such as laboratory studies characterizing a newly discovered virus or elementary particle, with results typically published in scientific journals. Paragraph 248(1)(b) (Applied Research) covers work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view, such as investigating how electrons behave in semiconductors to control conductivity or exploiting viral characteristics to develop a vaccine. Paragraph 248(1)(c) (Experimental Development)—the category under which the vast majority of corporate SR&ED claims are filed—covers work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto. Unlike basic or applied research, experimental development does not seek to advance pure scientific theory; rather, it advances technology (the practical application of scientific principles and engineering know-how) by resolving technological uncertainties that cannot be overcome through standard practice.

Under paragraph 248(1)(d) (Support Work), the definition of SR&ED includes work undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer with respect to eight exhaustive categories—engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research—strictly where that work is commensurate with the needs, and directly in support, of basic research, applied research, or experimental development described in paragraphs (a), (b), or (c) that is undertaken in Canada by or on behalf of the taxpayer. Support work is never SR&ED on its own; claimants must draw the project boundary around the experimental investigation and its commensurate support work, rather than around an entire commercial software build or manufacturing run.

Conversely, paragraphs 248(1)(e) to (k) expressly exclude from SR&ED any work with respect to: (e) market research or sales promotion; (f) quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes; (g) research in the social sciences or the humanities; (h) prospecting, exploring, or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum, or natural gas; (i) the commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product, or the commercial use of a new or improved process; (j) style changes (such as iterating a product's aesthetic form, finish, or proportions); or (k) routine data collection. As the CRA emphasizes, distinguishing eligible support work (such as testing or data collection under paragraph (d)) from excluded work (such as routine testing under paragraph (f) or routine data collection under paragraph (k)) depends entirely on purpose: data collection or testing conducted specifically to test an experimental hypothesis qualifies as support work, whereas data gathering or quality assurance conducted for normal commercial operations is statutorily excluded.

body.text: 2.2 The CRA "Why and How" Framework vs. The Common Law Five-Criteria Test

In its Guidelines on the eligibility of work for scientific research and experimental development (SR&ED) tax incentives (dated August 13, 2021; updated July 5, 2022), the CRA consolidated its administrative eligibility assessment into two mandatory requirements—the "Why" Requirement and the "How" Requirement—both of which must be satisfied for work to qualify.

First, the "Why" Requirement asks whether the work was conducted for the advancement of scientific knowledge or for the purpose of achieving a technological advancement. The CRA defines advancement as generating or discovering conceptual knowledge (such as predictive models or theories, rather than mere factual data or measurements) that advances the understanding of science or technology. New scientific or technological knowledge is required only when an objective scientific or technological uncertainty exists—that is, when it is unknown or uncertain whether a given objective can be achieved, or how to achieve it, due to an insufficiency in the combined available scientific or technological knowledge of the business's internal resources and publicly available sources. Characteristics pointing to insufficient technological knowledge include non-applicable existing design methods, non-conforming specifications, excessive unknowns or interacting variables, operating parameters outside normal ranges, interlocking system constraints, or economic/cost targets that standard methods cannot satisfy. Crucially, circumventing a technical obstacle with a workaround using available knowledge, or acquiring available knowledge through training, hiring consultants, or buying proprietary technology, fails the "Why" requirement. Conversely, because subsection 248(1) requires only that the work be undertaken "for the purpose of" achieving advancement, commercial or experimental failure still qualifies: work that proves a hypothesized approach does not work advances technological knowledge by ruling out that pathway.

Second, the "How" Requirement asks whether the work was conducted by means of a systematic investigation or search carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis. Simply following standard engineering procedures or carrying out work systematically is insufficient; rather, a systematic investigation requires: (1) generating an idea or hypothesis consistent with known facts that serves as a starting point toward resolving the problem; (2) testing that hypothesis by means of experiment or analysis (allowing the hypothesis to evolve and change iteratively based on test results); (3) developing logical conclusions based on the experimental or analytical findings; and (4) keeping contemporaneous evidence generated as the work progresses. As confirmed by the Federal Court of Appeal in National R&D Inc. v. Canada and Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. Canada, the CRA's "Why and How" framework does not depart from common law; it simply reorganizes the binding five-question test established in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen, with the "Why" requirement encompassing technical risk/uncertainty and technological advancement, and the "How" requirement encompassing hypothesis formulation, scientific method testing, and contemporaneous documentation.
3. Federal Investment Tax Credit (ITC) Rates, Thresholds, and Phase-Out Mechanics
3.1 Claimant Classifications: Qualifying CCPCs, ECPCs, and Other Taxpayers

Under Sections 127 and 127.1 of the Income Tax Act and the CRA's SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy (updated October 7, 2026), both the rate of the federal ITC (35% enhanced vs. 15% basic) and its cash refundability (100%, 40%, or 0%) depend on the claimant's legal status throughout the taxation year and whether the qualified expenditure is current or capital in nature.

For Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs), most stand-alone or associated CCPCs earn the enhanced 35% ITC rate on qualified current and capital SR&ED expenditures up to their annual expenditure limit ($6 million for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024; $3 million for taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024), and the basic 15% ITC rate on qualified expenditures exceeding their expenditure limit. Within the CCPC category, the CRA distinguishes three sub-categories for refundability purposes:

items: Qualifying Corporations (other than excluded corporations): Defined as a CCPC whose prior-year taxable income (combined with any associated corporations) did not exceed its qualifying income limit for the current year. Up to the $6 million expenditure limit, their 35% ITC is 100% refundable on current expenditures and 40% refundable on capital expenditures; above the expenditure limit, their 15% ITC is 40% refundable on both current and capital expenditures.

CCPCs (other than qualifying or excluded corporations): Up to the $6 million expenditure limit, their 35% ITC is 100% refundable on current expenditures and 40% refundable on capital expenditures; however, above the expenditure limit, their 15% ITC is non-refundable (0% refund).

Excluded Corporations: Up to the $6 million expenditure limit, their 35% ITC is 40% refundable on both current and capital expenditures, and above the expenditure limit, their 15% ITC is also 40% refundable on both current and capital expenditures.

body.text: For Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs)—a new category enacted by Bill C-15 for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024—the corporation must, throughout the taxation year, be resident in Canada, have a class of shares listed on a designated stock exchange (or have elected, or been designated by the Minister of National Revenue, to be a public corporation), and not be controlled directly or indirectly in any manner whatever by one or more non-resident persons (determined as if all shares owned by non-residents were owned by a single hypothetical person). Additionally, Canadian-resident corporations where all or substantially all of the shares are owned by one or more ECPCs are eligible under the ECPC rules. Qualifying ECPCs earn the enhanced 35% ITC on qualified expenditures up to their $6 million expenditure limit—with 100% cash refundability on current expenditures and 40% cash refundability on capital expenditures—and a 15% non-refundable ITC on qualified expenditures above the expenditure limit.

For all other corporations (including foreign-controlled subsidiaries, non-CCPC private corporations, and public corporations that do not qualify as ECPCs or exceed the phase-out limit), the federal ITC is a flat 15% non-refundable credit across all current and capital expenditures. Finally, individuals, unincorporated businesses, and certain trusts earn a 15% ITC that is 40% refundable on both current and capital expenditures. Because a partnership is not a taxpayer, it cannot claim an ITC or refund directly; instead, the ITC is calculated at the partnership level at the 15% basic rate and allocated to eligible partners under subsection 127(8), where partners that are qualifying corporations, individuals, or certain trusts can claim a 40% refund on their allocated ITC (while non-qualifying corporate partners receive a non-refundable credit).

body.text: 3.2 Expenditure Limit Phase-Out Formulas: Taxable Capital vs. Gross Revenue

Under subsections 127(10.2) to 127(10.6) as amended by Bill C-15, the $6 million annual expenditure limit for the 35% enhanced ITC is subject to two distinct phase-out structures—one based on taxable capital employed in Canada and one based on three-year average gross revenue.

Under the Taxable Capital Phase-Out Structure (the default test for CCPCs), for taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024, the $3 million expenditure limit was reduced by $0.075 for every $1 of prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada (on an associated-group basis) between $10 million and $50 million, reaching nil at $50 million. Under Bill C-15, for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the prior-year taxable capital phase-out thresholds (applied across the associated group) increased to between $15 million and $75 million, with the $6 million expenditure limit beginning to shrink only once prior-year taxable capital exceeds $15 million and becoming nil at $75 million. Under the formula in subsection 127(10.2), the expenditure limit equals $6 million × ($60 million − A) ÷ $60 million, where A is the amount (not exceeding $60 million) by which prior-year taxable capital exceeds $15 million, so the limit is reduced by $0.10 for every $1 of taxable capital above $15 million; the August 15, 2025 legislative draft, based on the interim $4.5 million limit, applied a reduction rate of $0.075 per $1 over the same $15 million–$75 million band. Associated CCPCs must share a single $6 million expenditure limit and file an allocation agreement under subsection 127(10.3) using T2 Schedule 49 (Form T2SCH49), which the CRA updated on May 29, 2026. Short taxation years and multiple taxation years ending in the same calendar year also proportionally reduce the expenditure limit.

Under the Gross Revenue Phase-Out Structure (mandatory for ECPCs and elective for CCPCs), an ECPC's access to the $6 million expenditure limit is phased out on a straight-line basis if the ECPC's average gross revenue over the three preceding fiscal years exceeds $15 million, and is completely eliminated when three-year average gross revenue reaches $75 million. For corporate groups preparing consolidated financial statements, gross revenue is the amount reported at the highest level of consolidation presented to shareholders, and all group members must share the single $6 million expenditure limit; for standalone corporations, gross revenue is the amount reported in annual financial statements prepared under GAAP. Crucially, for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, a CCPC (or associated group of CCPCs) may elect to have its expenditure limit determined using this three-year average gross revenue phase-out structure ($15 million to $75 million) instead of the taxable capital structure, allowing capital-intensive, pre-revenue CCPCs with more than $15 million in taxable capital to preserve their full $6 million enhanced expenditure limit.
3.3 Carryover Rules and Taxability of Federal and Provincial Credits

Earned federal ITCs are first applied under subsection 127(5) to reduce federal Part I income tax payable for the current taxation year. Any unused non-refundable ITC balance beyond the amount needed to reduce Part I tax to zero may be carried back up to 3 taxation years or carried forward up to 20 taxation years.

To prevent double benefits, both federal and provincial R&D tax credits interact with the taxpayer's taxable income and expenditure pools, but on different timelines. Federal SR&ED ITCs that are applied against tax payable or refunded in cash in a taxation year reduce the Section 37 deductible SR&ED expenditure pool (or are included in taxable income) in the following taxation year. Conversely, provincial and territorial R&D tax credits are treated as "government assistance" under paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsection 127(18), meaning they reduce both the federal Section 37 deductible expenditure pool (Form T661 Line 429) and federal Section 127 qualified expenditures (Form T661 Line 513 for current expenditures and Line 514 for post-December 15, 2024 capital property) in the current taxation year if received, entitled to be received, or reasonably expected to be received by the filing due date. However, when a claimant elects the Proxy Method, the portion of a provincial R&D tax credit that relates to the notional Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) does not reduce the federal Section 37 pool; instead, it is included directly in taxable income in the year it is received or applied. Furthermore, if a claimant subsequently repays government or non-government assistance or a contract payment that previously reduced its pool or qualified expenditures, the repayment is added back to the Section 37 pool on Line 445 and added to the qualified expenditure pool on Line 560 in the year of repayment to earn an ITC.
4. Qualifying SR&ED Expenditures (QREs), Calculation Methods, and Cost Categories

To earn an SR&ED deduction or ITC, a cost must fall into one of the exhaustive categories set out in Section 37 and Regulation 2900: salaries or wages, materials consumed or transformed, overhead and other expenditures (or the Prescribed Proxy Amount), SR&ED contracts and third-party payments, or post-December 15, 2024 capital expenditures and equipment lease costs.
4.1 Overhead Election: The Proxy Method vs. The Traditional Method

In Part 3, Section A of Form T661, a claimant must elect annually between the Proxy Method (Line 160) and the Traditional Method (Line 162) to calculate SR&ED expenditures and overhead. Under the CRA's Traditional and Proxy Methods Policy (updated March 30, 2022), this election is made on a year-by-year basis; once Form T661 is filed for a taxation year, the chosen method cannot be changed for that year, and if no selection is made on the form, the CRA defaults the claim to the Traditional Method.

When a claimant elects the Proxy Method under clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B) and the Prescribed Proxy Amount Policy (updated April 28, 2022), they do not track or claim actual SR&ED overhead expenditures on Form T661 (entering "0" in Box 758 of Part 6). Instead, overhead expenses (such as office supplies, utilities, clerical support salaries, and general-purpose office equipment) remain deducted as ordinary business expenses, and the claimant calculates a notional Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) in Part 5 of Form T661 that flows to Line 502 in Part 4 to earn an SR&ED ITC. Under subsection 2900(4) of the Income Tax Regulations, the PPA is strictly 55% of the salary base. Auditors must verify that claimants do not apply a 65% rate, which was the historical proxy rate for 2012 and earlier taxation years (before transitioning to 60% prorated for 2013 and 55% since 2014). The salary base (computed in Part 5, Section A, Line 818) comprises the eligible salaries and wages of employees directly engaged in SR&ED in Canada (plus permissible foreign SR&ED wages), excluding taxable benefits, bonuses, remuneration based on profits, and employment inducements (subtracted on Line 812 for non-specified employees and excluded on Line 852 for specified employees under Regulation 2900(9)). Additionally, under subsection 2900(6), the PPA cannot exceed an overall cap equal to the total amount deducted in computing business income for the year, less deductions under sections 20, 24, 26, 30, 32, 37, 66 to 66.8, and 104 of the Act, and less any outlay or expense for the use of or right to use a building other than a special-purpose building.

Conversely, when a claimant elects the Traditional Method under subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(II) and the SR&ED Overhead and Other Expenditures Policy (updated October 14, 2022), no salary base or PPA is calculated. Instead, the claimant must specifically identify, track, allocate, and substantiate actual overhead and other expenditures on Line 360 of Form T661 (and allocate them by project in Box 758 of Part 6 for taxation years ending after 2020). Under Regulations 2900(2)(c) and 2900(3), an overhead expenditure qualifies under the Traditional Method only if it is either: (a) directly related to the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada and incremental—meaning it would not have been incurred if the SR&ED had not occurred (Regulation 2900(2)(c)); or (b) the cost of maintenance and upkeep of SR&ED premises, facilities, or equipment, or other expenditures directly related to providing those premises, facilities, or equipment that would not have been incurred had they not existed (Regulation 2900(3)). Unlike the notional PPA, eligible Traditional Method overhead is included in both the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool and Section 127 qualified expenditures for ITC purposes.

body.text: 4.2 Salaries and Wages, Specified Employees, Foreign Work, and the 180-Day Unpaid Rule

Under subsection 37(8), Regulation 2900(2)(b), and the CRA's SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy (updated January 28, 2025), eligible labour expenditures consist of "salary or wages"—defined in subsection 248(1) as income from an office or employment—incurred for employees who directly undertake, supervise, or support the prosecution of SR&ED. Under the Proxy Method, claimable salaries on Line 300 (non-specified employees) and Line 305 (specified employees) are restricted strictly to employees "directly engaged" in SR&ED, which refers to hands-on technical tasks determined by actual duties performed rather than job title. Eligible hands-on tasks include experimentation and analysis; commensurate support work under paragraph 248(1)(d); operating machinery or feeding raw materials for an experiment under technical supervision; first-line technical supervision that directs the technical course of ongoing SR&ED (work beyond first-line supervision or non-technological management does not qualify); technical input into SR&ED contract administration; technological planning and feasibility studies for claimed ongoing SR&ED projects; and preparing internal technical documentation. Clerical and administrative staff (such as payroll, HR, accounting, purchasing, or sales personnel) are never considered directly engaged under the Proxy Method, though they may qualify as incremental overhead under the Traditional Method. Under Regulation 2900(5), if an employee spends all or substantially all (90% or more) of their time on SR&ED in the year, 100% of their eligible salary is included (subject to specified employee caps).

Allowable salary or wages include regular gross pay, vacation pay, statutory holiday pay, sick leave pay, pay in lieu of termination notice, cash outlays for taxable benefits under section 6 (or non-cash taxable benefits if reasonably estimated, net of GST/HST/PST input tax credits, and not claimed elsewhere as a business expense), employment inducements or non-competition payments for services rendered, and—solely for non-specified employees—bonuses and remuneration based on profits. Strictly excluded from SR&ED salary or wages are dividends (paid on T5 slips as a return on share capital rather than employment income under subsection 248(1); founders paid exclusively in dividends generate $0 in SR&ED claims), employer payroll contributions and related benefits (the employer's share of CPP/QPP, EI, WSIB/CNESST, pension/superannuation plans, group medical/dental/optical insurance, and savings plans), stock option benefits, retiring allowances, and extended vacation or sick leave where no duties are performed.

Special statutory restrictions apply to "specified employees", defined in subsection 248(1) as any employee who owns, directly or indirectly at any time during the year, 10% or more of the issued shares of any class of the corporation or a related corporation (counting shares held by non-arm's-length relatives, proportionate partnership/fixed trust interests, and 100% of shares held by a discretionary family trust of which the employee is a beneficiary), or who otherwise does not deal at arm's length with the corporation (such as a spouse or child of a controlling shareholder, even with 0% shareholding). Specified employees are subject to three cumulative restrictions:

items: Complete Exclusion of Bonuses and Profit-Based Pay (Subsection 37(9)): Any bonus or remuneration based on profits paid or payable to a specified employee is completely excluded from SR&ED expenditures on Line 305 and earns zero credit.

Direct SR&ED Salary Cap of 5× YMPE (Subsections 37(9.1) to 37(9.4)): Under subsection 37(9.1), the maximum SR&ED salary claimable for a single specified employee in a taxation year is capped at 5 times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) determined under section 18 of the Canada Pension Plan, prorated by the number of days the individual was a specified employee in the year. As illustrated in Canadian CPA guidance, with a YMPE of $74,600, this 5× YMPE ceiling equals $373,000 ($74,600 × 5). Under subsections 37(9.2) to 37(9.4), if a specified employee works for two or more associated corporations, no salary can be claimed by any of them unless all associated corporations file an agreement allocating a single 5× YMPE cap among the group.

Proxy Salary Base Cap of 75% and 2.5× YMPE (Regulations 2900(7) and 2900(8)): In Part 5 of Form T661 (Lines 850 to 860), subsection 2900(7) limits the salary of a specified employee that can enter the Proxy Salary Base to the lesser of: (a) 75% of the total salary or wages incurred for that employee in the year (excluding bonuses, profit-based pay, and taxable benefits) (Line 856); and (b) the formula 2.5 × A × B / 365 (2.5 times the YMPE prorated by days employed, or $186,500 at a $74,600 YMPE) (Line 858). Under Regulation 2900(8), associated corporations must share a single 2.5× YMPE proxy salary base cap per specified employee.

body.text: For SR&ED Work Performed Outside Canada (Subsections 37(1.4) and 37(1.5)), while general foreign R&D under subsection 37(2) is ineligible for the Section 37 pool and ITC, a claimant may claim "permissible salary or wages" on Line 307 (non-specified) and Line 309 (specified) up to 10% of the total salaries and wages directly attributable to SR&ED carried on in Canada, provided all five statutory criteria are met: (1) the foreign work was performed directly by an employee (never a contractor); (2) the employee was a resident of Canada at the time the expense was incurred; (3) the work related to a business of the claimant; (4) the work outside Canada was an integral part of, and solely in support of, SR&ED carried on in Canada by the claimant; and (5) the salary or wages paid are not subject to an income or profits tax from another country.

Finally, under the 180-Day Unpaid Expenditure Rule, any salary or wages (or other current expenditure) incurred in a taxation year that is not paid within 180 days of the end of that taxation year is deemed not to have been incurred in that year and must be deducted on Line 315 (for unpaid wages) or Line 520 (for other unpaid current expenditures) of Form T661. When the amount is subsequently paid in a later taxation year, it may be claimed on Line 310 (wages) or Line 500 (other current expenses, or 80% thereof for arm's-length contracts), strictly provided that the unpaid expenditure was reported on Form T661 for the original year of accrual within the 18-month reporting deadline.
4.3 Materials Consumed vs. Materials Transformed and ITC Recapture

Under Regulation 2900(2)(a) and the CRA's Materials for SR&ED Policy (updated March 27, 2026), claimants using either the Proxy or Traditional method may claim the cost of materials consumed (Form T661 Line 320) or materials transformed (Form T661 Line 325) in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada. To qualify as "materials for SR&ED", an item must satisfy a strict three-part tangibility requirement: (1) the raw materials, substances, or items must be physical and tangible (in a solid, liquid, or gaseous state); (2) the term "thing" refers to a tangible physical object; and (3) at a given moment in the SR&ED process, the material must compose the body of a tangible thing on which the SR&ED is carried out, or that results from the SR&ED being carried out. Consequently, broken or used lab supplies (petri dishes, beakers, flasks, pipettes), cleaning supplies, CDs/DVDs, used lubricants, and general utilities (water, electricity, natural gas, propane) do not compose the body of the object under experimentation; they are excluded from materials under both methods and can only be claimed as overhead under the Traditional Method (Line 360). Conversely, seed, growth media, agar, fungal cultures, and test-plot fertilizers or herbicides compose the body of the experimental object and qualify as materials consumed.

Eligible material cost is the laid-down cost, comprising invoice cost, customs and excise duties, transportation, acquisition, and storage costs; for internally manufactured goods or inventory used in SR&ED, cost includes laid-down raw materials plus direct labour and the share of production overhead properly chargeable to production (even if the claimant uses the Proxy Method). Purchases of materials from non-arm's-length suppliers are restricted for ITC purposes to the actual cost incurred by the non-arm's-length supplier, excluding intercompany profit (Form T661 Line 542). Crucially, materials purchased for future use or held in inventory can only be claimed in the taxation year in which they are actually consumed or transformed in SR&ED (or when testing on duplicate prototype copies is completed), not when purchased or constructed.

The distinction between materials consumed (Line 320) and materials transformed (Line 325) governs exposure to ITC Recapture under subsections 127(27) to 127(36) and the CRA's Recapture of SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy (updated October 14, 2022). Materials consumed are destroyed, absorbed, used up, or rendered virtually valueless (disposed of as waste or scrap) during SR&ED testing, triggering no recapture. Materials transformed (including experimental production batches, custom products, commercial assets, animals/growing things, or duplicate copies of a prototype damaged during testing but sold to a client) retain commercial value or are incorporated into another property. If property that generated an SR&ED ITC (including transformed materials, ASA capital equipment, or shared-use equipment) is subsequently sold or converted to commercial use, subsections 127(27) to 127(36) claw back the ITC by adding the recaptured credit directly to the taxpayer's Part I tax payable in the year of sale or conversion (while allowing the prior year's recaptured ITC to be added back to the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool on Line 453 in the following year). Notably, if a claimant orders a part from an arm's-length supplier for $12,000, the full $12,000 acquisition cost is subject to recapture upon commercial sale or conversion, whereas if the claimant manufactures that same part in-house, recapture applies only to the cost of the raw materials transformed and not to the in-house salaries or overhead expended to fabricate it.
4.4 Subcontractors, Non-Arm's-Length Contracts, and Third-Party Payments
Payments to external parties for SR&ED performed in Canada are governed by three distinct statutory regimes depending on the relationship between payer and performer and who controls the research:

items: Arm's-Length SR&ED Contracts (Form T661 Line 340): Under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01) and the Contract Expenditures for SR&ED Performed on Behalf of a Claimant Policy (updated March 30, 2022), payments to an arm's-length contractor to perform basic research, applied research, experimental development, or commensurate support work in Canada on behalf of the claimant are 100% included in the Section 37 deduction pool. For Section 127 ITC purposes, however, subparagraph (a)(ii) of "qualified expenditure" in subsection 127(9) limits inclusion to 80% of the contract expenditure (requiring a 20% reduction on Line 529 of Form T661). Furthermore, the contractor must be a "taxable supplier" (a Canadian resident, a Canadian partnership, or a non-resident / non-Canadian partnership carrying on business through a permanent establishment in Canada); contract amounts paid to non-taxable foreign suppliers are deducted on Line 528 and earn no ITC. Under Bill C-15, contract expenditures and third-party payments incurred after December 15, 2024 are no longer reduced by related capital expenditures of the SR&ED performer.

Non-Arm's-Length (NAL) SR&ED Contracts (Form T661 Line 345 & Form T1146): Under subsection 37(13), work performed by a non-arm's-length party is recognized as SR&ED if it would have been SR&ED had the payer performed it directly, allowing the expenditure into the Section 37 pool on Line 345. However, under paragraph (f) of "qualified expenditure" in subsection 127(9), NAL contract payments are excluded from the payer's qualified expenditures for ITC purposes (deducted on Line 541). To transfer the ITC to the payer, the NAL performer and payer must jointly file Form T1146 (Agreement to Transfer Qualified Expenditures Incurred in Respect of SR&ED Contracts Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length, updated May 15, 2026) under subsection 127(13), transferring the performer's qualified expenditures (including any PPA) from the performer (Line 540) to the payer (Line 508). Additionally, excess assistance across a non-arm's-length group must be allocated using Form T1145 (updated May 15, 2026) and entered on Line 538.

Third-Party Payments (Form T661 Line 370 & Form T1263): Under subparagraphs 37(1)(a)(i.1), (ii), and (iii) and the Third-Party Payments Policy (updated March 30, 2022), a claimant may claim payments made to an approved university, college, research institute, approved association, granting council, another Canadian-resident corporation, or a tax-exempt non-profit SR&ED corporation under paragraph 149(1)(j) for SR&ED carried on in Canada related to the claimant's business, provided the claimant is entitled to exploit the results. Unlike contracts (where the payer controls the work, holds exclusive rights, and accounts on an accrual basis), third-party payments involve research controlled by the recipient institution with non-exclusive/preferential exploitation rights for the payer, are accounted for on a cash basis, are included at 80% for ITC purposes (Line 529), and require attaching a completed Form T1263 (Third-Party Payments for SR&ED) for each payment.

body.text: 4.5 Restored Capital Expenditures, Shared-Use Equipment, and Equipment Leases (Bill C-15)

Between January 1, 2014 and December 15, 2024, capital property and equipment lease costs were completely excluded from SR&ED deductions and ITCs. Bill C-15 restored the eligibility of capital expenditures and equipment lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024, governed by the CRA's updated SR&ED Capital Expenditures Policy (updated June 29, 2026), SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy (updated June 8, 2026), and SR&ED Shared-Use Equipment Policy (updated May 22, 2026).

Under paragraph 37(1)(b) and subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(III), an expenditure to acquire new or used depreciable property (reported on Form T661 Line 390) qualifies as an SR&ED capital expenditure if the property is acquired and available for use (under subsection 37(1.2)) after December 15, 2024, and at the time of acquisition the claimant intended either to use it during all or substantially all (ASA — 90% or more) of its operating time in its expected useful life for SR&ED in Canada, or to consume all or substantially all (90% or more) of its value in the performance of SR&ED in Canada (note that one CRA web summary describes the threshold as "more than 90%", while the statutory policy and updates define ASA as "90% or more"). Claimants must substantiate intended use with contemporaneous evidence from acquisition (project plans, purchase approvals, commissioning notes, and usage logs) and list the 20 most expensive depreciable properties acquired after December 15, 2024 on Line 262 and Box 780 of Form T661. Deducted SR&ED capital expenditures are deemed to have been allowed as Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) and must not be claimed on T2 Schedule 8.

If newly acquired depreciable property (acquired after December 15, 2024) is used for both SR&ED and commercial activities, but is used primarily (more than 50% and less than 90% of its operating time) for SR&ED in Canada, it qualifies as Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) under subparagraph (a)(iii) of "qualified expenditure" in subsection 127(9). SUE does not enter the Section 37 deduction pool, but earns an SR&ED ITC on 25% of its capital cost in the first period (first-term SUE) and 25% in the second period (second-term SUE, up to 50% total across the two periods), reported in Boxes 788, 790, 792, 794, and 796 of Form T661. Excluded from SR&ED capital and SUE ITCs are land (non-depreciable), buildings and leasehold interests in buildings (excluded under paragraph 37(8)(d)), used (second-hand) depreciable property (which qualifies for the Section 37 income deduction but is a prescribed expenditure disallowed from earning an ITC on Line 530), and—under the Proxy Method and SUE rules—general-purpose office equipment or furniture (GPOEF).

A major financial planning distinction applies between leased equipment (Form T661 Line 350) and purchased capital equipment (Form T661 Line 390) incurred after December 15, 2024. Under the restored lease rules, lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024 for equipment used 90% or more (ASA) for SR&ED in the year are claimed at 100% as current lease expenditures on Line 350 under both the Proxy and Traditional methods. If leased equipment (other than GPOEF) is used primarily (more than 50% to under 90%) for SR&ED, Proxy Method claimants can claim 50% (1/2) of the lease cost on Line 350 under subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(VI), whereas Traditional Method claimants claim the proportional SR&ED percentage for equipment used less than 90% as overhead on Line 360. Because eligible equipment lease costs are current expenditures, a qualifying CCPC or ECPC within its $6 million limit receives a 100% cash refund on the 35% federal ITC earned on leased equipment. By contrast, on purchased capital equipment (Line 390), only 40% of the 35% federal ITC is paid as a cash refund, while the remaining 60% of the federal ITC is non-refundable and must be applied against federal tax payable or carried back 3 years / forward 20 years.

5. Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Incentives Across Canada

Eight Canadian provinces and one territory offer dedicated R&D tax credits or tax-system grants that stack with the federal SR&ED program. Following the enactment of federal Bill C-15 in March 2026, provincial responses ranged from full statutory harmonization in British Columbia and a sweeping structural consolidation in Québec (the CRIC) to the retention of independent provincial expenditure caps in Ontario, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Atlantic Canada, and the Yukon.

body.text: 5.1 Ontario: OITC, ORDTC, OBRITC, and the Multi-Layer Assistance Grind

Corporations with a permanent establishment in Ontario performing eligible SR&ED in Ontario can stack up to three provincial tax credits administered by the CRA alongside their federal T2 return. First, the Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC)—governed by section 96 of the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario) (S.O. 2007, c. 11, Sched. A) and Ontario Regulation 37/09, and claimed on T2 Schedule 566 (flowing to Schedule 5 Line 468)—provides an 8% fully refundable tax credit on qualified Ontario SR&ED expenditures up to an annual expenditure cap of $3,000,000 (for a maximum annual credit of $240,000, shared among associated corporations and prorated for short taxation years). Ontario did not adopt the federal increase to a $6 million expenditure limit, meaning Ontario SR&ED spending between $3 million and $6 million earns the 35% federal ITC but no OITC. Furthermore, the $3 million OITC expenditure limit phases out under two prior-year associated-group tests: it declines linearly when prior-year federal taxable income is between $500,000 and $800,000 (eliminated at $800,000), or when prior-year specified/taxable capital employed in Canada is between $25,000,000 and $50,000,000 (eliminated at $50,000,000). Regarding post-December 15, 2024 capital expenditures in Ontario, the 2026 Ontario Economic Outlook and Fiscal Review (October 29, 2026) confirmed that capital expenditures on property acquired on or after December 16, 2024 are eligible for both the OITC and the ORDTC, a change that took effect in Ontario automatically when the corresponding federal amendments in Bill C-15 received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026. Under subsection 96(14) of the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario), a corporation may formally waive all or part of its current-year OITC so that it does not reduce the federal expenditure pool.

Second, the Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC)—claimed on T2 Schedule 508 (flowing to Schedule 5 Line 416, with recapture on Line 277)—provides a 3.5% non-refundable tax credit on eligible Ontario SR&ED expenditures. Unlike the OITC, the ORDTC has no annual expenditure limit, no taxable income or taxable capital phase-out, and is open to all corporations (including large or foreign-controlled corporations) with an Ontario permanent establishment, with unused credits carrying back 3 years and forward 20 years. Third, the Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC)—claimed on T2 Schedules 568 and 569 (flowing to Schedule 5 Line 470)—provides a 20% fully refundable tax credit on qualified contract expenditures paid to an eligible Ontario research institute (university, college, or hospital research institute), capped at $20,000,000 of qualified expenditures per year ($4,000,000 maximum credit).

When stacking the OITC, ORDTC, and federal ITC on $1,000,000 of eligible Ontario current SR&ED spending by a qualifying CCPC, specialized Ontario CPA guides citing ontario.ca and canada.ca establish the following four-step statutory order of operations (the OITC is government assistance that reduces the ORDTC base, whereas neither the ORDTC nor the federal ITC reduces the OITC base):

items: Compute the OITC First (8% Refundable): Apply 8% directly to the $1,000,000 Ontario expenditure base, generating $80,000 in refundable OITC.

Compute the ORDTC Second (3.5% Non-Refundable): Reduce the $1,000,000 Ontario base by the $80,000 OITC to yield an ORDTC base of $920,000, and multiply by 3.5% to generate $32,200 in non-refundable ORDTC (total combined Ontario credits of $112,200, or 11.22%).

Compute the Federal SR&ED ITC Third (35% Refundable): Reduce the $1,000,000 federal expenditure base by both provincial credits ($1,000,000 − $80,000 − $32,200 = $887,800), and multiply by 35% to generate $310,730 in refundable federal ITC.

Aggregate Combined Recovery: The claimant earns $422,930 in total combined credits (42.293% of spend), of which $390,730 ($80,000 OITC + $310,730 federal ITC, or 39.073% of spend) is refunded immediately in cash.

body.text: 5.2 Québec: The Unified CRIC Regime (Post-March 25, 2025) and Revenu Québec Administration

In its 2025–2026 Budget delivered on March 25, 2025, the Government of Québec replaced eight existing innovation tax measures—the four former R&D tax credits (including the 14% base / 30% enhanced R&D salary credit on Form RD-1029.7), the tax credit for in-house industrial design activities, the tax credit for technological adaptation services, the tax holiday for foreign researchers, and the tax holiday for foreign experts—with the Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC / Crédit d'impôt pour la recherche, l'innovation et la commercialisation). Applying to taxation years (or partnership fiscal periods) beginning after March 25, 2025 (with legacy credits restricted to taxation years beginning on or before March 25, 2025), the CRIC represents $2,412.6 million in projected provincial support over five years ($106.0M in 2026–2027, $715.9M in 2027–2028, $769.5M in 2028–2029, and $821.2M in 2029–2030).

While Québec's definition of R&D remains harmonized with the federal SR&ED definition under subsection 248(1) (and the CRA conducts the scientific review of R&D work), the CRIC expands eligible activities to include pre-commercialization activities carried out in Québec in conjunction with R&D performed by or on behalf of the corporation. Eligible pre-commercialization activities encompass: (1) tests, technological validations, and studies performed to meet regulatory requirements to obtain initial approval or certification for commercializing an innovation; (2) product design, including form and aesthetic development, improved functionality, and material selection; and (3) quality control activities for a product or process strictly where they relate to implementing a quality control system required for initial regulatory approval or certification.

Rather than varying rates by corporate asset size, the CRIC provides a size-neutral, 100% refundable tax credit to any corporation with an establishment in Québec carrying on business there, equal to 30% on the first $1,000,000 of qualified expenditures above the annual exclusion threshold, and 20% on all qualified expenditures exceeding that $1,000,000 cap (with partnership claims earning 20%). Qualified CRIC expenditures include 100% of salaries and wages paid to employees, 50% of amounts paid to subcontractors for contracts carried out in Québec, 50% of payments made to eligible Québec public research centres, research consortia, or university entities, and 100% of property/equipment acquisition costs (excluding land, buildings, or rights to use land/buildings, and prohibiting double-claiming equipment under the 15%–25% Tax Credit for Investment and Innovation, C3i). The annual exclusion threshold is the greater of $50,000 or the sum of the applicable basic personal amount under Québec's personal income tax system ($18,571 in 2025; $18,952 in 2026) for each eligible employee, prorated by the percentage of time each employee spent on eligible R&D and pre-commercialization activities. Claimants file Form RD-222 (Deduction of R&D Expenditures) and Form RD-1029.8.CR (or RD-1029.8.CR-T; alongside the CO-1029.8.36 series) with Revenu Québec. Additionally, Québec's 30% Tax Credit for the Development of E-Business (CDAE — Form CO-1029.8.36.DA) (23% refundable / 7% non-refundable in 2025, requiring an Investissement Québec certificate) is replaced for fiscal years starting after December 31, 2025 by the CDAEIA for companies integrating artificial intelligence features (22% refundable / 8% non-refundable in 2026, 21% / 9% in 2027, and 20% / 10% from 2028), and the same employee hours cannot be claimed under both CRIC and CDAE/CDAEIA.
5.3 British Columbia, Alberta, the Prairies, Atlantic Canada, and the Territories

In British Columbia, the B.C. SR&ED Tax Credit—governed by Part 6 of the Income Tax Act (B.C.) and Bill 2 (Budget Measures Implementation Act, 2026), and claimed on Form T666 (Schedule 5 Line 674 refundable / Line 659 non-refundable) within 18 months of year-end—was made permanent in B.C. Budget 2026 (repealing its prior September 1, 2027 expiry date) and expressly harmonized with federal Bill C-15. For taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024, qualifying CCPCs and Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) with a B.C. permanent establishment earn a 10% refundable tax credit on up to $6,000,000 of qualified B.C. SR&ED expenditures (phasing out between $15 million and $75 million of prior-year taxable capital, and including restored capital expenditures), while expenditures above the limit or by other corporations earn a 10% non-refundable credit (carrying back 3 years and forward 10 years). B.C. video game and VR/AR developers can also stack the 17.5% refundable B.C. Interactive Digital Media Tax Credit (IDMTC) with SR&ED.

In Alberta, the Innovation Employment Grant (IEG)—administered through the corporate tax system on AT1 Schedule 29—provides a refundable grant of 8% on eligible Alberta R&D expenditures up to the corporation's base spending level (its average qualifying Alberta R&D spending over the preceding two years), plus an enhanced 20% rate (8% base + 12% incremental payment) on eligible spending exceeding that two-year average base, up to $4,000,000 in annual R&D spending. The IEG phases out incrementally for corporations with prior-year taxable capital between $10,000,000 and $50,000,000, and updated guidance issued on June 30, 2026 confirmed that Alberta retains its separate $4 million cap while providing reconciliation instructions for the revised federal Form T661.

In Saskatchewan (T2 Schedule 403), CCPCs earn a 10% refundable credit on their first $2,000,000 of qualifying expenditures incurred on or after December 16, 2024 (doubled from $1 million), while excess expenditures and non-CCPCs earn a 10% non-refundable credit, subject to a $1,000,000 total annual credit cap. Manitoba (T2 Schedule 380) offers a 15% R&D tax credit on eligible current and depreciable capital expenditures (excluding buildings), which is 100% refundable for R&D conducted under an eligible contract with a qualifying Manitoba research institute and 50% refundable / 50% non-refundable for other eligible R&D. Finally, Nova Scotia (T2 Schedule 340), New Brunswick (T2 Schedule 360), and Newfoundland and Labrador (T2 Schedule 301 / Form T1129) each provide a 15% fully refundable R&D tax credit, while Yukon provides a 15% fully refundable credit plus an additional 5% (20% total refundable credit) on eligible expenditures paid or payable to Yukon University.

body.text: 6.2 The Strict 18-Month Statutory Reporting Deadline and Subsection 220(2.2)

Under subsection 37(11), paragraph 127(9)(m), and the CRA's SR&ED Filing Requirements Policy (updated January 28, 2025), the SR&ED reporting deadline is 12 months after the filing due date of the claimant's income tax return for the taxation year in which the expenditures were incurred. For corporations (whose T2 return is due 6 months after year-end), this provides a strict reporting window of 18 months from the end of the taxation year (e.g., June 30, 2027 for a December 31, 2025 year-end). For individuals, the deadline is 17.5 months from the end of the tax year; for partnerships, Form T661 must be filed with the partnership information return no later than 12 months after the earliest of all filing due dates for the return of income of any member for the tax year in which the partnership's fiscal period ends; and for tax-exempt corporations, Form T661 is due on or before the filing due date for their return. Under subsection 220(2.2) of the Income Tax Act, there is no statutory mechanism to extend the 18-month SR&ED reporting deadline; if an expenditure is not reported on prescribed Form T661 by the 18-month mark, it is permanently disallowed for federal and provincial SR&ED purposes.
6.3 The CRA Optional Pre-Claim Approval Process (Launched April 1, 2026 — Form T1322)

Introduced in Budget 2025 and launched by the CRA on April 1, 2026, the optional SR&ED Pre-Claim Approval Process enables eligible businesses to obtain an upfront technical eligibility determination from the CRA before commencing work or incurring major R&D costs. To qualify, the applicant must be a CCPC, another Canadian corporation, or a Canadian partnership, have annual gross business income of less than $25 million, and be in good standing with the CRA. Applications may cover up to 3 projects of new or recently started work that have never appeared in a prior SR&ED claim and do not involve issues under litigation. The application follows a four-step procedure:

items: Request a Case Number: Complete the online web form on Canada.ca; existing SR&ED claimants in good standing receive a case number within 2 business days via My Business Account, while all other businesses are contacted within 5 business days by phone.

Complete and Upload Form T1322: Complete Form T1322 (Application for Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) pre-claim approval), including project identification (Lines 010–032) and a description of the objective and scientific or technological uncertainty on Line 042 (maximum 500 words), and upload Form T1322 with up to 10 supporting documents in My Business Account.

Attend the CRA Technical Meeting: Within 4 weeks of submission, meet with a CRA Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) for an estimated 2 to 5 hours (mandatory for new claimants; at the RTA's discretion for existing claimants in good standing).

Receive Determination and File Form T661: Within 8 weeks of submitting a complete application, the CRA issues a formal determination that remains valid for up to 3 years. While pre-claim approval provides technical approval rather than a financial audit of expenditures, refundable claims selected for review that contain only pre-approved projects (reported on Form T661 Lines 212 and 214) have their expenditure review processing time cut in half from 180 days to 90 days.

body.text: 6.4 Claim Preparer Penalties (Subsections 162(5.1)–(5.3)) and Gross Negligence Penalties

In Part 9 of Form T661, claimants must disclose complete information regarding any external claim preparer (including contingency fee rates, which typically run 10% to 25% of the credit, or flat/hourly billing arrangements), or complete Lines 935, 970, and 975 if prepared entirely in-house. Under subsection 162(5.1) of the Income Tax Act, if complete and accurate claim preparer information is missing from Part 9, a $1,000 penalty applies for which the claimant and the claim preparer are jointly and severally (together or separately) liable, subject to the due diligence defence in subsection 162(5.2) and definitions in subsection 162(5.3) (auditors should note that subsection 163(2.4) relates to foreign property reporting penalties such as Form T106, whereas the Form T661 Part 9 penalty is governed by subsections 162(5.1)–(5.3)). In addition, overstated SR&ED claims remain subject to the CRA's Gross Negligence Penalty on Overstated SR&ED Claims Policy (updated January 28, 2025).
7. Landmark Jurisprudence and CRA Audit Precedents

Canadian courts interpret the SR&ED provisions of the Income Tax Act under Section 12 of the Interpretation Act to give the statute "such fair, large and liberal construction and interpretation as best ensures the attainment of its objects" (Consoltex Inc. v. The Queen, (1997), 97 D.T.C. 724 (TCC)), while strictly enforcing the taxpayer's evidentiary burden under the five-question common law test established by Chief Justice Bowman in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen ([1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520 (TCC)) and endorsed by the Federal Court of Appeal in C.W. Agencies Inc. v. The Queen (2001 FCA 393) and RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen (99 D.T.C. 5087 (FCA)).

In National R&D Inc. v. Canada (2020 TCC / FCA) and Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. Canada (2019 TCC / 2021 FCA), the Federal Court of Appeal rejected arguments that Criterion 3 of Northwest Hydraulic (adherence to the scientific method) lacked a statutory basis or was superseded by the CRA's 2021 "Why and How" guidelines, confirming that CRA guidelines are non-binding and that the Northwest Hydraulic five-element test remains the law of Canada. In Joel Theatrical Rigging Contractors (1980) Ltd. v. Her Majesty the Queen (2017 TCC 6), Justice Sommerfeldt defined "routine engineering" (para. 17) as "techniques, procedures and data that are generally accessible to competent professionals in the field", defined a "hypothesis" (para. 26) as a "statement to be tested by an experiment or a trial", and denied the claim because the team lacked engineering credentials or external specialists and failed to record exact weights and descent times during trials. Similarly, Canafric Inc. v. His Majesty the King (2023 TCC 108) confirmed that missing knowledge must be lacking in the broader scientific or technological knowledge base, not merely unknown to the claimant.

Conversely, in Manning Canning Kitchens Inc. v. His Majesty the King (2024 TCC 159; original Judgment December 13, 2024, Amended Reasons January 17, 2025), Justice Scott Bodie allowed the appeal of a Toronto food and beverage company that developed "Chrisoda", a room-temperature shelf-stable canned beverage containing unpasteurized cold-pressed juice and vinegar that initially caused test cans to explode from microbial fermentation. By collaborating with an experienced food science consultancy (Hale Foods), formulating and testing hypotheses around "Chiber" (a white button mushroom extract from Chinova Bioworks previously used only in dairy), and systematically logging Brix, pH, carbonation, and concentrate ratios, the taxpayer satisfied all five Northwest Hydraulic criteria. Crucially, the Court held that contemporaneous records need not be decipherable on a standalone basis by an outside layperson; their primary purpose is to enable the researchers conducting the work to track progress, evaluate hypotheses, and determine next steps.

body.text: 8. Comprehensive Audit Verification Checklist for Canadian SR&ED Claimants

items: Confirm Taxation Year Cut-Offs and the $6 Million Expenditure Limit: Verify whether the taxation year began after December 15, 2024 to apply the $6,000,000 enhanced 35% expenditure limit and the $15M–$75M taxable capital or three-year average gross revenue phase-out bands under Bill C-15 (filing T2 Schedule 49 for associated corporations).

Evaluate Optional Pre-Claim Approval (Form T1322): For eligible corporations or partnerships with gross business income under $25 million starting new projects, submit Form T1322 via My Business Account to obtain an 8-week technical determination valid for up to 3 years and access the 90-day expenditure review track.

Audit the Proxy Overhead Calculation (55% PPA Rate & Specified Employee Caps): Confirm that Part 5 of Form T661 applies the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount rate under Regulation 2900(4), excludes all bonuses, profit-based pay, taxable benefits, and dividends from the salary base, caps specified employee direct salary at 5× YMPE ($373,000) under subsection 37(9.1), and caps specified employee proxy salary base at the lesser of 75% of total salary and 2.5× YMPE ($186,500) under Regulation 2900(7).

Segregate Restored Capital Equipment, SUE, and Equipment Leases: For depreciable property acquired and available for use after December 15, 2024, substantiate the 90% ASA test with acquisition records and usage logs, report the top 20 properties on Line 262 and Box 780, model the 40% cash refundability on capital ITCs vs. 100% cash refundability on current lease costs (Line 350), claim 25% first-term / second-term SUE in Boxes 788–796, and exclude used equipment and buildings from ITC calculations (Line 530).

Reconcile the 180-Day Unpaid Rule and Bona Fide Government Loans: Remove any wages (Line 315) or current expenditures (Line 520) unpaid 180 days after year-end on Form T661 so they remain claimable when paid, and verify under Bill C-69 that bona fide government loans with reasonable repayment terms made after December 31, 2019 are not deducted as government assistance.

Model Provincial R&D Stacking and Assistance Grinds: Apply the exact provincial rules for the relevant permanent establishment—including Québec's CRIC (30% on the first $1M above the $50,000 / basic personal amount exclusion threshold, 20% above $1M, plus pre-commercialization expenses on Forms RD-222 and RD-1029.8.CR for tax years starting after March 25, 2025), B.C.'s permanent 10% credit ($6M limit on Form T666), Ontario's 8% OITC ($3M cap on Schedule 566) and 3.5% ORDTC (Schedule 508), or Alberta's 8%/20% IEG ($4M cap on AT1 Schedule 29).

Structure Technical Narratives and Contemporaneous Evidence to Jurisprudence Standards: Draft Part 2 Section B of Form T661 and maintain project records demonstrating why uncertainties could not be resolved by routine engineering (Joel Theatrical Rigging; Canafric) and preserving dated quantitative logs of hypotheses and trials (Northwest Hydraulic; Manning Canning Kitchens).

Verify Part 9 Claim Preparer Disclosures and the 18-Month Statutory Deadline: Complete Part 9 of Form T661 accurately to avoid the $1,000 joint-and-several penalty under subsection 162(5.1), and file Form T661 (Version 26) and Schedule T2SCH31 before the non-extendable 18-month reporting deadline under subsections 37(11), 127(9)(m), and 220(2.2).
